extracted.subtask_description: A newsroom style guide for inclusive, accurate and sensitive language around religion, race, gender, disability and other identity-related topics; provides preferred terms, cautions and usage examples. Intended to guide reporting, headlines and copy decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eid al-Adha
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronounced “EED-uhl-AH-duh.” A Muslim festival that commemorates the willingness of Abraham to sacrifice his son; observed with prayers and a feast, whether or not they are on hajj. Shifts dates every year because Muslims use a lunar calendar of about 354 days. Commences with the sighting of the new moon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See hajj.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eid al-Fitr
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronounced “EED-uhl-FIT-uhr.” A joyous Islamic holiday marking the end of Ramadan, observed with communal prayers, donations to charity and special meals. Fasting is forbidden on this day. Dates shift yearly with lunar calendar and it commences with sighting of the new moon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Ramadan.

rubrics_metrics.name: elderly
rubrics_metrics.description: Use this word carefully and sparingly. The term is appropriate only in generic phrases that do not refer to specific individuals (e.g., concern for the elderly). Describing a person as elderly is bad form, although the generalized category might not be offensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If intent is to show deterioration of faculties, cite a graphic example and attribute it to someone (per Associated Press guidance). Avoid using elderly to describe named individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emancipation Proclamation
rubrics_metrics.description: Lincoln’s 1863 proclamation and executive order encouraging slaves in the South to become contrabands behind Union lines; applied only in the areas of the 10 Southern states that had seceded and did not address slavery in Union border states. Tied slavery to preserving the Union and set the stage for the 13th Amendment but did not end slavery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note historical limits and that some celebrate the end of slavery on Juneteenth (June 19, 1865) when Union troops arrived in Galveston to enforce the proclamation. See Angel Island; internment, Japanese.

rubrics_metrics.name: eñe, ñ
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Spanish alphabet, ñ is an additional letter (called eñe), not just an n with an accent; pronounced “enye.” Substituting plain n changes words. Sounds like the middle sound in canyon; Spanish word for canyon is cañon.

rubrics_metrics.name: English-only movement
rubrics_metrics.description: An effort to make English the official language of the United States; about half the states have adopted English-only laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opponents say such laws are unnecessary, divisive and even racist.

rubrics_metrics.name: epicanthic fold
rubrics_metrics.description: See eye shape. The term refers to a distinctive eyelid feature sometimes called an epicanthic fold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to eye shape entry for guidance and cautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: epilepsy/epileptic fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Epilepsy is a chronic neurological disorder with recurrent, unprovoked seizures; manifests differently among individuals. Treated commonly with medication but also medical devices, surgery, diet and emerging therapies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to someone as having epilepsy only if relevant and formally diagnosed by a licensed professional. Use people-first language (has epilepsy) rather than calling someone an epileptic. Use 'seizure' as preferred term; avoid 'fit' or 'epileptic fit'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episcopal Church
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of the Anglican Communion; officially the Protestant Episcopal Church in the United States of America. Two national governing bodies: Executive Council and General Convention. Capitalize titles before a name and lowercase otherwise. Some U.S. congregations have broken ties and affiliated with Anglican bishops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify whether a bishop is Anglican or Episcopal in stories about disputes. Use titles: presiding bishop (Most Rev.), other bishops (the Rt. Rev.), priests/deacons (the Rev.), deans (Very Rev.), archdeacons (the Venerable). Women and men in religious communities are called brother or sister and may be ordained.

rubrics_metrics.name: equality
rubrics_metrics.description: Equality means ensuring every individual has equal opportunity and that no one should have poorer life chances because of birthplace or background. Recognizes historical discrimination against certain groups and the need to correct injustices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eskimo
rubrics_metrics.description: A member of indigenous peoples of Alaska and other Arctic regions. The term is controversial and should be used with caution because it is considered derogatory in many places; preferred terms vary by region (Inuit in much of Canada; Alaska Native in U.S. federal law since 2016).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask individuals or community leaders what they prefer to be called; be aware some Alaskans accept 'Eskimo' while others prefer 'Inuit' or local designations.

rubrics_metrics.name: ethnic
rubrics_metrics.description: Commonly used to describe things from countries outside North America/Western Europe or cultures other than White; like 'exotic' it connotes otherness and can be marginalizing and offensive. Should never be used to describe a person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer specific country or culture (e.g., Vietnamese food); for multiple cultures use international music, global food or world cuisine. Note academic field 'ethnic studies' is acceptable. See referenced essays and reporting critiquing use of 'ethnic'.

rubrics_metrics.name: ethnic group
rubrics_metrics.description: Caution — vague. A group of people who self-identify because of geographical, linguistic, cultural, religious or other ties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically used as synonym for race; use more specific language where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: ethnicity, mention of
rubrics_metrics.description: A person’s ethnicity should not be mentioned unless relevant; same applies to sexual orientation and religion. Derogatory terms or slurs may not be used unless directly bearing on the news and then only with senior editor approval. Avoid stereotypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Race and ethnicity may be relevant in: crime stories (detailed suspect descriptions properly attributed), biographical/announcement stories (reserve mention of race/ethnicity for significant historic 'firsts' only). See race.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evangelical Lutheran Church in America
rubrics_metrics.description: The largest Lutheran denomination in the U.S.; ELCA is acceptable on second reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse with the Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod, which is smaller and more conservative. See Lutheran.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Order 9066
rubrics_metrics.description: Signed Feb. 19, 1942 by FDR after Pearl Harbor; led to internment of about 117,000 people of Japanese heritage (two-thirds U.S. citizens). Cabinet divided and Office of Naval Intelligence had affirmed loyalty of Japanese Americans. Supreme Court repeatedly affirmed constitutionality but Congress in 1983 called it 'a grave injustice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides historical context and link to text of the order. See Angel Island; internment, Japanese.

rubrics_metrics.name: exotic
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid. When describing women of Asian and Pacific Islander heritage it often implies departure from a white norm and is pejorative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See essay by Rachel Kuo and other referenced critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: eye shape, reference to
rubrics_metrics.description: Misnomer — all human eyeballs have the same shape. The distinctive 'Asian' feature is the epicanthic fold, found in all races but not universal among Asians. Terms like 'slanted' or 'slitty' are racially derogatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain relevance for the reader/viewer if discussing the fold (e.g., plastic surgery). Avoid irrelevant references (e.g., an Asian basketball player’s supposed reduced field of vision). See epicanthic fold.

rubrics_metrics.name: fag, faggot
rubrics_metrics.description: A pejorative term for a gay male and extremely offensive when used as an epithet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use only in a quotation if there is a compelling reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: family (LGBT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper term for identifying a family led by LGBT parents. Identify parents’ sexual orientation only when germane. Do not use 'gay families.' Mention genetic relationships or conception techniques only when germane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See parent.

rubrics_metrics.name: fat
rubrics_metrics.description: See obese, obesity.

rubrics_metrics.name: fatwa
rubrics_metrics.description: A legal pronouncement issued by an Islamic scholar; there is no central authority. The expert must have rigorously studied the Quran and issues fatwas aware of all elements of the case. Pertains only to Muslims and is not binding in secular settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fatwas usually give religious guidance; dangerous or death-fatwas are rare.

rubrics_metrics.name: felon, offender
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid these labels when referring to people convicted of crimes because they define people by the crime. Use people-first language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specific formulations: 'Jane Doe was convicted of felony robbery'; 'John Doe is registered as a sex offender in Iowa'; 'Joe Doe was on trial for criminal loitering'; 'Jane Doe was placed on probation'; 'On parole in New Mexico, John Doe…' Follow The Marshall Project recommendations to avoid dehumanizing labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: female/feminine pronouns, male/masculine pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all people who use she/her are women, and not all who use he/him are men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the term 'pronouns' and forms like 'she/her pronouns' or 'he/him pronouns' rather than equating pronouns with gender identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filipino/Pilipino
rubrics_metrics.description: Refers to an inhabitant of the Philippines. Filipino American refers to those who share its heritage and culture. Some prefer 'Pilipino' because Tagalog lacks an 'F' sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Tagalog; note historical naming (named after King Philip II of Spain).

rubrics_metrics.name: First Nations
rubrics_metrics.description: Term for Aboriginal peoples of Canada who are neither Métis nor Inuit; came into usage in 1970s–80s and generally replaced 'Indian' in Canada. Not widely used in the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Updated Feb 2021.

rubrics_metrics.name: First World
rubrics_metrics.description: Outdated Cold War term referring to developed capitalist countries (North America, Western Europe, Japan, Australia). With end of Cold War, the 'Three World' model is no longer relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'developed world' and 'developing world' instead. See Third World.

rubrics_metrics.name: fixer
rubrics_metrics.description: In journalism, a fixer helps foreign correspondents arrange interviews, translate, interpret and offer in-country expertise. Some consider the term demeaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider alternatives like 'local reporting partner', 'local correspondent' or 'local journalist'. Updated March 2021.

rubrics_metrics.name: flip
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid. Pejorative for Filipino.

rubrics_metrics.name: fortune cookie
rubrics_metrics.description: Origin almost certainly Japanese; references exist in Japanese literature (1878 image). China and Japan do not have a tradition of dessert following a meal.

rubrics_metrics.name: FTM / MTF / FTN / MTN / FT* / MT*
rubrics_metrics.description: Acronyms describing transgender or transsexual individuals: first letter assigned birth sex, 'T' for 'to' (transition), third letter is destination gender; '*' indicates inclusivity of variations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fu Manchu
rubrics_metrics.description: Caution — stereotype. Fictional evil genius popularized in early 20th-century fiction and films; described with racist tropes and formed basis for 'yellow peril' stereotypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid stereotypical uses and be aware of historical racist context.

rubrics_metrics.name: fundamentalism, fundamentalist
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally a Christian movement emphasizing biblical inerrancy; term has come to be associated with any religious reactionary movement and is often misapplied as a pejorative to conservative Christians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best to avoid the words unless the group applies the terms to itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: gay
rubrics_metrics.description: Refers to men attracted to other men; preferred over 'homosexual' which connotes clinical context. Avoid using as a singular noun. For women, 'lesbian' is generally used; when possible ask which term a person prefers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To include both, use 'gays and lesbians'. In headlines where space is limited, 'gay' is acceptable to describe both. See homosexual, lesbian.

rubrics_metrics.name: geezer
rubrics_metrics.description: Ageist terminology. Avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: gender assigned at birth (GAAB), MAAB, FAAB
rubrics_metrics.description: The gender a person is born as; 'gender assigned at birth' acknowledges it may not be the person's true gender. MAAB = male assigned at birth; FAAB = female assigned at birth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See transgender.

rubrics_metrics.name: gender binary
rubrics_metrics.description: The assumption that there are only two distinct genders (male and female). Many see this as a false dichotomy given intersex, transgender and agender people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See agender, intersex, transgender.

rubrics_metrics.name: gender dysphoria
rubrics_metrics.description: DSM-V replaced 'Gender Identity Disorder' with 'Gender Dysphoria' in 2013 and changed diagnosis criteria. Necessity of psychiatric diagnosis remains controversial; both psychiatric and medical authorities recommend individualized medical treatment (hormones and/or surgeries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some advocates see DSM listing as necessary for insurance coverage. Ask people with gender dysphoria which pronouns they prefer.

rubrics_metrics.name: gender expansive
rubrics_metrics.description: Increasingly used for people who challenge cultural expectations about gender roles, identities or expressions. Some identify within man/woman categories, some as neither, some as both/mixed; may use gender-neutral pronouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See agender, genderqueer, transgender. Updated Feb 2021.

rubrics_metrics.name: gender expression
rubrics_metrics.description: External manifestations of gender through name, pronouns, clothing, haircut, behavior, voice or body characteristics; cues change over time and by culture. Transgender people typically seek to align gender expression with gender identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See gender-expansive, transgender.

rubrics_metrics.name: gender fluidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Conveys a flexible range of gender expression that may change over time (even day to day). Gender-fluid children may not feel confined by boy/girl categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask people who are gender fluid which pronouns they prefer. See gender-expansive.

rubrics_metrics.name: gender identity
rubrics_metrics.description: One’s internal, deeply held sense of gender. For transgender people, it does not match sex assigned at birth. Most people identify as man or woman; some do not fit neatly into either.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gender identity is not visible to others. See gender expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender Identity Disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: Outdated term — avoid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See gender dysphoria.

rubrics_metrics.name: gender nonconforming
rubrics_metrics.description: Describes people whose gender expression differs from conventional expectations. Not all gender-nonconforming people are transgender, nor are all transgender people gender nonconforming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only use if someone self-identifies as gender nonconforming; ask which pronouns they prefer.

rubrics_metrics.name: gender normative
rubrics_metrics.description: Refers to people whose sex assignment at birth corresponds to their gender identity and expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See cisgender, cis.

rubrics_metrics.name: gender role
rubrics_metrics.description: Set of roles, activities, expectations and behaviors assigned to females and males by society; culture recognizes two basic gender roles: masculine and feminine. People who step out of assigned roles are sometimes referred to as transgender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note other cultures may have three or more gender roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: gender spectrum
rubrics_metrics.description: A model that breaks the gender binary and accounts for infinite variations of gender.

rubrics_metrics.name: gender transition
rubrics_metrics.description: Process by which transgender people change physical and sexual characteristics from those associated with sex at birth; may include name changes, legal document changes, hormone therapy, and sometimes surgery or other body modifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not synonymous with 'sexual reassignment.' Avoid outdated term 'sex change.' Use specific procedure names only when appropriate; avoid 'mastectomy' for transmasculine chest surgery—prefer 'chest reconstruction' or 'chest masculinization'.

rubrics_metrics.name: gender variant
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid unless used in academic writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: gender-affirming care/transition-related medical care
rubrics_metrics.description: Broad term for healthcare transgender people may pursue including counseling, hormone replacement therapy, and surgeries. Not all transgender people pursue all forms; many never receive care due to cost, access or choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing about medical care, general language is usually better. Use official name of a surgery/treatment when appropriate; avoid mastectomy for transmasculine chest surgery—use 'chest reconstruction surgery' or 'chest masculinization surgery.' See Trans Journalists Association guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: gender-bender, gender-bending
rubrics_metrics.description: An individual who intentionally does not conform to predominant binary gender roles or expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use only if self-referential or in quotation with compelling reason. As adjective, 'gender-bending'.

rubrics_metrics.name: gender-neutral pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Some people don’t feel traditional pronouns reflect their gender identities; transgender, genderqueer and others may adopt new pronouns. If a person doesn't identify as male or female, ask which pronouns they use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides alternatives to traditional pronouns. Updated March 1, 2021.

rubrics_metrics.name: genderqueer
rubrics_metrics.description: Used by some whose gender identity/expression falls outside 'man' and 'woman'; not a synonym for transgender and should be used only if self-identified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask which pronouns they use; see gender-neutral pronouns, agender, transgender, gender non-conforming.

rubrics_metrics.name: genocide
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberate killing of a large group, especially defined groups (national, ethnical, racial or religious) with intent to destroy the group. The term is specific and refers to coordinated actions aiming at destruction of essential foundations of a group. Established in law by the 1948 UN Convention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use accurately; historical context and examples given (Armenian, Holocaust, Rwandan, Cambodian, Bosnian, etc.). Understand legal definition includes acts (a)–(e) listed in the Convention.

rubrics_metrics.name: gentile
rubrics_metrics.description: In Judaism, anyone who is not a Jew; usually a reference to Christians. Some Mormons use the term to describe non-Mormons.

rubrics_metrics.name: gerontology/geriatrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Gerontology studies social, psychological and biological aspects of aging; geriatrics is medical specialty studying diseases, disabilities and health of older people.

rubrics_metrics.name: ghetto
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically used for city sections inhabited by poor people or minorities; avoid because of negative connotations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use neighborhood name, section, district or quarter instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: God
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize in reference to all monotheistic religions (God, God the Father, Holy Ghost, Holy Spirit). Lowercase personal pronouns (him, he). Many Christians consider God beyond gender; be sensitive and avoid gender-defining pronouns when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Orthodox Jews write 'G-d' to avoid erasing God’s name; journalists should respect this practice in quotes but otherwise use God.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good Friday
rubrics_metrics.description: In Christianity, Good Friday commemorates the crucifixion of Jesus Christ and falls just before Easter Sunday; part of Holy Week.

rubrics_metrics.name: good name
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrase in India where 'What is your good name?' literally asks for a person's name; it's a literal translation of Hindi 'Aap ka shubhnam?'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of literal-translation pitfalls in cross-cultural questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gospel, gospel
rubrics_metrics.description: From Old English 'Godspell' meaning 'good news'; refers to the New Testament books Matthew, Mark, Luke and John. Capitalize when referring to those books; lowercase otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: grandfather in, grandfather clause
rubrics_metrics.description: A way to exempt people from a legal change because of prior conditions (e.g., existing properties are exempt). Originated in the American South to enfranchise poor white people and disenfranchise Black people by waiving voting requirements for descendants of men who voted before 1867.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use with caution due to racist origins; consider alternatives like 'legacy' in some contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Great Migration, the
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-Reconstruction move from the South to the North (c.1916–1970) in which some 6 million African Americans moved to Northeast, Midwest and West seeking opportunity and fleeing violence and segregation. They still faced segregation in destination cities.

rubrics_metrics.name: green card
rubrics_metrics.description: United States Permanent Resident Card (actually pink). Allows an immigrant to live and work permanently in the U.S.; not citizenship. Asking U.S.-born Latinos or Puerto Ricans if they have a green card can be insulting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See immigrant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gullah
rubrics_metrics.description: A creole blending Elizabethan English and African languages developed in isolated Sea Islands plantation communities; flourished due to isolation and persisted after emancipation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Creole.

rubrics_metrics.name: gurdwara
rubrics_metrics.description: A Sikh place of worship that houses the Guru Granth Sahib (Sikh scripture).

rubrics_metrics.name: guru
rubrics_metrics.description: Teacher, particularly in Hinduism, Sikhism and Buddhism; informally used as any knowledgeable guide or mentor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gypsy
rubrics_metrics.description: Used to indicate Roma people; the word has negative connotations and many Roma see it as a racial slur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'Roma people' unless people self-identify as 'Gypsies' (capitalize). Avoid casual/pejorative uses and the slang 'gyp' (likely derived from Gypsy).

rubrics_metrics.name: hadith
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronounced 'ha-DEETH.' A report about a saying, action or tradition of Muhammad and companions; can be singular or plural. Viewed as explanations of the Quran and second only to it as a source of guidance and Shariah.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two most reliable collections are by Bukhari and Muslim (9th century scholars). Use term accurately.

rubrics_metrics.name: hair, African American or Black
rubrics_metrics.description: When describing a person’s hair, ask what style it is; don't assume. Black hair has a variety of styles and textures (afro, bald/shaved, braids, cornrows, dreadlocks/locs, extensions, Jheri curl, twists, weave).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware Black hairstyles have been political and personal; use questions about hair to open conversation and understand context. See referenced video 'Five Questions About Black Hair.'

rubrics_metrics.name: hajj
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronounced 'hahj.' The Islamic pilgrimage to Mecca; fifth of Five Pillars. Every Muslim who is physically/financially able is expected to make hajj at least once. Takes place during the 12th month with specific rites during a five-day period. Dates move yearly with lunar calendar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Festival of Eid al-Adha occurs at the end of hajj. Word typically not capitalized. A hajji is a person who has undertaken the pilgrimage. See Eid al-Adha.

rubrics_metrics.name: halakhah
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronounced 'ha-la-KHAH.' Jewish law — rules and practices governing many aspects of life, defined by scripture and teachings and interpreted by rabbis for each generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: halal
rubrics_metrics.description: In Arabic, lawful/permitted in Islam. Refers to foods, objects and activities sanctioned by Islamic teaching. Halal foods are permissible; slaughter process requires invoking God’s name and cutting throat to drain blood. Pork, blood, intoxicants and alcohol are not halal.

rubrics_metrics.name: hamesh hand
rubrics_metrics.description: Hamesh is the Hebrew word for hamsa in Arabic, meaning five or 'five fingers of the hand.' In Jewish/Israeli culture the hamsa is often adorned with a Star of David or Hebrew letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: hamsa
rubrics_metrics.description: A palm-shaped symbol for good luck or protection that predates Islam; seen in many cultures and adopted by people of many traditions. Some Muslims call it the 'hand of Fatima.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often worn as jewelry and is non-religious in many contexts.
